column3: Address of where someone lives: 住 "live" + 址 "site". It is the word on forms and for a person's home. 地址 is the general word for any address and is more common in speech. 址 has 土 "earth" and 止, which gives the sound.
column7: Please write down your address.

column3: Mother tongue, native language: 我的母語是英語. 母 is "mother" and 語 "language". For the language of a country or people, 語 is also the ending: 英語, 日語.
column7: My native language is English.

column3: Clock that hangs on a wall or stands on a table. 鐘 originally means "bell" (it has 金 "metal" on the left), and 時鐘 is a "time bell". A wristwatch is a 手錶 with a different character, 錶, and an alarm clock is a 鬧鐘. Counted with 個.
column6: Kètīng lǐ yǒu yī ge dà shízhōng.
column7: There is a big clock in the living room.

column3: Night, evening, a slightly literary word for the time after dark, good for describing: 夜晚很安靜 "the night is quiet". In everyday speech people say 晚上, and 夜裡 or 半夜 for "in the night". The sun 日 in 晚 shows time, as in 時 and 明; 夜 has 夕 "evening" at the bottom.
column7: The seaside is quiet at night.

column3: Breakfast, a little more old-fashioned and more used in the Chinese style of breakfast: 早點 stands sell soy milk, 燒餅 and so on. The usual word is 早餐. Do not confuse it with 早點 meaning "a bit earlier", which is just 早 and 一點: 早點睡 "go to bed earlier".
column7: We eat breakfast outside.

column3: Maternal grandfather, your mother's father. 外 means "outside": on the mother's side the family is "outside" the father's line. The father's father is 爺爺. It is also how you speak to him. 外婆 is the matching word for your mother's mother.
column7: My maternal grandfather lives in Tainan.

column3: Maternal grandmother, your mother's mother, the partner of 外公. 外 is "outside" because she is from the mother's side of the family. Her husband is 外公, and your father's mother is 奶奶. The 婆 has 女 "woman" at the bottom and 波 for the sound.
column6: Wàipó zuò de cài hěn hǎochī.
column7: My grandmother's cooking is delicious.

column3: Father's elder brother. Children also use it for older men who are friends of their father: 王伯伯. The father's younger brother is 叔叔, so 伯 and 叔 tell you whether he is older or younger than your father. The second 伯 is neutral.
column7: My uncle is coming to our house today.

column3: Father's elder brother, used mostly in compounds: 伯父 and 伯母 for an uncle and his wife, and 大伯 for the eldest. It is also the word for the third of the five ranks of old nobility (伯爵 "count"). 亻 is "person" and 白 gives the sound, which matches well (bái and bó).
column7: My uncle is a doctor.

column3: Father's elder brother. It is also a respectful way to address or talk about an older man, a friend of your father: 李伯父. Close to 伯伯, but more formal. The wife is 伯母, and 父 is "father".
column7: My uncle lives in Kaohsiung.

column3: Wife of father's elder brother. It is also a polite address for a friend's mother or any woman about the age of your mother: 伯母好. The partner of 伯父. 母 is "mother", the same as in 母語.
column6: Bómǔ zuò de cài hěn hǎochī.
column7: My aunt's cooking is delicious.

column3: Father's younger brother, mostly met in 叔叔 and 叔父. It is also how children address any man about their father's age. The word list gives a second reading for Taiwan, shú. The 小 inside it can remind you "younger", and 伯 is the elder brother.
column7: My uncle works in Taipei.

column3: Father's sister, your paternal aunt. 姑姑 and 姑媽 are both used, and an older sister of your father is 大姑. 姑 is 女 "woman" with 古 "old" beside it; the aunt is the "old woman" of the father's side. The second 姑 is neutral.
column7: My aunt is very fond of children.

column3: Shy, bashful, also "to be embarrassed": 他很害羞, 別害羞. It is used of a person who becomes shy in front of others, and works as an adjective or a verb: 她害羞地笑了. 害 is "harm" and 羞 is "shame", so it is "feeling shame".
column4: 他在人多的时候很害羞。
column5: 他在人多的時候很害羞。
column6: Tā zài rén duō de shíhou hěn hàixiū.
column7: He is very shy when there are many people.

column3: To teach, in the sense of working as a teacher: 他在學校教書. It is a verb with its object (書), so the pieces can come apart. To teach a subject or a person, use 教 alone: 教英文, 教學生. Here 教 is read jiāo; as a noun in 教育 it is jiào.
column7: She teaches at an elementary school.

column3: Way of doing something, method, often of a person's action: 這種作法不好 "this way of doing it is not good". 做法 is the other common way to write it, the more usual one on the mainland, and means the same. 作 "do, make" + 法 "method".
column6: Tā de zuòfǎ bù tài hǎo.
column7: His way of doing it is not very good.

column3: Example, case, precedent, seen in 例子 "example", 例如 "for example", 舉例 "give an example", 比例 "proportion". It does not stand alone in speech. Ask for one with 請你舉一個例子. 亻 gives "person" and 列 "row" gives the sound, which has lost its final -e (liè and lì).
column6: Qǐng nǐ jǔ yī ge lìzi.
column7: Please give an example.

column3: To study, go to school. 念書 is a common spoken word for studying and being a student: 他在台北念書 "he is studying in Taipei", 念了三年書. 讀書 means the same. Like other verb-object words it can be split: 念了很多書. For reading aloud, 念 alone is used.
column7: He is studying in Taipei.

column3: Mathematics, literally "number study": 數 + 學. Names of school subjects are built this way: 數學, 化學, 地理. 數學課 is the class and 數學老師 the teacher. This 數 is read shù as a noun; as the verb "count" it is shǔ.
column6: Wǒ de shùxué bù tài hǎo.
column7: I am not very good at math.

column3: Grammar: 文 "writing" + 法 "method, rules". The mainland more often says 語法, which is understood in Taiwan too. A grammar point is a 文法重點, and a grammar mistake a 文法錯誤.
column6: Zhōngwén de wénfǎ bù tài nán.
column7: Chinese grammar is not too difficult.

column3: To remove, get rid of, and "to divide". You mostly meet it in 除了: 除了...以外 "except, besides". 除了中文，他還會說日語 "besides Chinese he also speaks Japanese". With 也 or 還 it means "in addition to", and with 都 or 沒 it means "except". On the left, 阝 is a mound or city; 余 gives the sound.
column4: 除了中文，他还会说日语。
column5: 除了中文，他還會說日語。
column6: Chúle Zhōngwén, tā hái huì shuō Rìyǔ.
column7: Besides Chinese, he also speaks Japanese.

column3: Elementary school in Taiwan, short for 國民小學: 他在念國小. The grades are 國小 (six years), 國中 (junior high) and 高中 (senior high). The mainland says 小學 for this, which Taiwan uses too, especially in the name 小學生.
column7: His younger brother is in elementary school.

column3: Spring break, the school holiday in spring, around early April in Taiwan (it includes the Tomb Sweeping holiday). 春 + 假 "holiday". Other holidays are named the same way: 暑假 "summer vacation", 寒假 "winter vacation". The phrase for taking it is 放春假 or 有春假.
column7: We are going to Taitung for spring break.

column3: Vacation, leave, in 放假 "have a holiday", 請假 "ask for leave", 暑假, 寒假, 假日. The same character is read jiǎ in the meaning "fake, false" (真假 "true or false"). The reading tells you which. 亻 and 叚: the second part gives the sound, and the meaning "borrow, false".
column7: I am off tomorrow.

column3: Roommate, the person who shares your room or apartment: 室 "room" + 友 "friend". Mostly of students sharing a dorm or a rented room: 我的室友. Someone sharing a whole apartment with you is also a 室友.
column7: My roommate is Japanese.

column3: A seat, a place, at a table, a theater or a restaurant: 有位子嗎？ "Is there a seat?", 找位子 "find a seat", 讓位子 "give up a seat". 座位 is the more formal word and means the same. 位 is the place where a person 亻 stands 立.
column7: Is there a seat here?

column3: Hardworking, diligent, used of studying: 他很用功 "he studies hard", 用功讀書. For a hardworking employee, 認真 or 努力 fit better. It is used as an adjective and a verb, and takes 很 or 不太: 不太用功. 用 "use" + 功 "effort".
column7: He studies very hard.

column3: Bedroom. 房間 is the everyday word for any room, and 臥室 is also used for "bedroom" in writing. 臥房 has 臥 "to lie down" and 房 "room". 臥 is a person 人 with an eye 臣 looking down, who is lying.
column6: Wǒ de wòfáng zài èr lóu.
column7: My bedroom is on the second floor.

column3: Bathroom, the room with the bath or shower: 浴 "bathe" + 室 "room". 洗澡 "take a bath" happens in the 浴室. It is also the word for a public bathhouse.
column7: There is hot water in the bathroom.

column3: A study, the room at home for working and reading: 書 "book" + 房 "room". Counted with 間: 一間書房. It can also mean a "studio".
column7: Dad is reading in the study.

column3: Dining table: 餐 "meal" + 桌 "table", the table where the family eats. Things on the table take 上: 餐桌上. A restaurant's table is just 桌子. Counted with 張: 一張餐桌.
column6: Cānzhuō shang yǒu sān ge cài.
column7: There are three dishes on the dining table.

column3: Cabinet, cupboard, in 櫃子 and compounds: 衣櫃 "wardrobe", 書櫃 "bookcase", 鞋櫃 "shoe cabinet", and 櫃檯 "counter". 木 "wood" shows what it is made of, and 貴 gives the sound (guì).
column7: The books are in the cabinet.

column3: The countryside, a village as opposed to the city: 我外婆住在鄉下. Often used with a warm tone, for the place where grandparents live: 回鄉下. 下 is neutral here. 鄉 holds an old picture of two people feasting; its sense of "village" came later.
column7: My grandmother lives in the countryside.

column3: Mosquito, in 蚊子 and compounds: 蚊香 "mosquito coil", 蚊帳 "mosquito net". 虫 "insect" is the meaning part, and 文 the sound, which matches exactly (wén). Insect words in general have 虫 on the left.
column7: There are many mosquitoes in summer.

column3: Mosquito. Being bitten is 被蚊子咬: 我被蚊子咬了. The mosquito spray is 防蚊液, and 蚊子 can be said for each one: 一隻蚊子. 子 is neutral.
column7: I got bitten by a mosquito.

column3: To sweat, literally "flow sweat". A verb with its object, so it splits: 流了很多汗 "sweated a lot". 流 "flow" and 汗 "sweat" each have the water mark 氵. Also 滿頭大汗 "sweat all over the head".
column7: You sweat after exercise.

column3: Pillow, counted with 個: 一個枕頭. 枕 has the wood 木 on the left, and 冘 gives the sound. 頭 is neutral. The verb "to rest the head on" is also 枕.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng yào yī ge xīn zhěntou.
column7: I would like a new pillow.

column3: Slippers, flip-flops: 拖 "drag" + 鞋 "shoe". At home people often take off their shoes at the door and put on slippers: 換拖鞋. Counted with 雙: 一雙拖鞋. Beach sandals are also 拖鞋, "dragged" shoes.
column7: Please change into slippers when you come in.

column3: Soap: 肥 "fat" + 皂, an old word for the soapy substance. A bar is 一塊肥皂. For washing the body or hands, 香皂 "scented soap" is also said. 洗手 goes with it: 用肥皂洗手.
column7: You have to wash your hands with soap.

column3: Toothpaste: 牙 "tooth" + 膏 "paste". Counted with 條 (a tube): 一條牙膏. 膏 is also the word for ointment (藥膏) and for sticky pastes in general. You squeeze it with 擠: 擠牙膏.
column6: Zhè tiáo yágāo kuài yòngwán le.
column7: This tube of toothpaste is almost used up.

column3: Toilet paper, and in Taiwan the general word for the plain paper in a bathroom or on a restaurant table. Facial tissues are 面紙 in Taiwan, 紙巾 on the mainland. In many buildings used paper goes in the bin, not the toilet; check for the sign. 衛生 "hygiene" + 紙 "paper".
column7: There is no toilet paper left in the bathroom.

column3: Basket, in 籃子 and in 籃球 "basketball", where the "basket" is the hoop. 竹 "bamboo" at the top, since baskets were woven of it, and 監 gives the sound. 菜籃 is a shopping basket.
column7: Let's go play basketball.

column3: A basket, usually small: 菜籃子 "shopping basket", 一個籃子. It holds things you carry: 籃子裡有水果. 子 is neutral.
column6: Lánzi lǐ yǒu hěn duō shuǐguǒ.
column7: There is a lot of fruit in the basket.

column3: A holiday, a day off: weekends and public holidays count: 假日 are the days when shops and the 夜市 are crowded. 國定假日 is a public holiday. 假 here is read jià "vacation" and 日 is "day".
column6: Jiàrì yèshì de rén hěn duō.
column7: On holidays the night market is crowded.

column3: To jog: 慢 "slow" + 跑 "run". Used as a verb for the activity: 去慢跑 "go jogging", 在公園慢跑. 跑 has 足 "foot" for meaning and 包 for the sound (bāo and pǎo). Plain "run" is 跑步.
column4: 我每天早上去公园慢跑。
column5: 我每天早上去公園慢跑。
column6: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang qù gōngyuán mànpǎo.
column7: I go jogging in the park every morning.

column3: A picnic, also "to have a picnic": 野 "wild, outdoors" + 餐 "meal". 去野餐 "go on a picnic", 在公園野餐. A mat for it is a 野餐墊. 野 is 里 with 予, where 里 is a village and fields.
column7: Let's go on a picnic on Sunday.

column3: To chat, a spoken verb. It is used alone, doubled or with 一: 聊聊, 聊一聊 "have a chat", and with 天 as 聊天. 聊 can be followed by the topic: 聊工作 "chat about work". The doubled and 一 forms soften it, like 看一看. In writing, 聊 also has older meanings (for the time being, somewhat) that you do not need yet.
column7: Let's have a chat.

column3: Musical instrument: 樂 "music" + 器 "utensil, device". Here 樂 is read yuè "music"; the same character is lè "happy", as in 快樂. The verb depends on the instrument: 彈 for strings and keyboards (彈吉他, 彈鋼琴), 吹 for winds, 拉 for the violin. The old character shows strings on a piece of wood.
column7: What instrument can you play?

column3: Guitar, a loanword whose characters are only used for the sound (吉 usually means "lucky"). The verb is 彈: 彈吉他, and 吉他手 is a guitarist. Counted with 把: 一把吉他.
column7: He can play the guitar.

column3: Teahouse, a place where you sit and drink tea, sometimes with snacks and a view. In Taiwan a quiet, traditional one is also called 茶藝館. 館 is a public building or shop: 飠 "food" and 官, as in 餐館 and 圖書館.
column7: We are drinking tea at the teahouse.

column3: Teahouse, the same word as 茶館 with the northern 兒 ending. Taiwan Mandarin uses that ending far less, so in Taiwan you will mostly see and say 茶館. The final r is added to the last syllable: cháguǎnr.
column7: Let's go and sit in the teahouse.

column3: Party, a loanword from English: 派 sounds like "par" and 對 like "-ty", with 對 "pair, facing" as a loose fit for people getting together. Used for lively parties: 開派對 "throw a party", 生日派對 "birthday party". A quiet gathering is more likely to be a 聚會.
column7: We are having a party this weekend.

column3: Three things: a piece, 一塊蛋糕 "a piece of cake"; "one yuan" in speech, 一塊錢 (in Taiwan one NT dollar); and "together", 一塊去, a more northern way of saying 一起. 塊 is the measure word for pieces, lumps and coins, and has 土 "earth" on its left.
column7: I ate a piece of cake.

column3: Time difference, jet lag. 有時差 "have jet lag", 調時差 "get over jet lag", and also the plain difference between two places: 台灣和日本有一個小時的時差. 差 here is read chā "difference".
column4: 台湾和日本只有一个小时的时差。
column5: 台灣和日本只有一個小時的時差。
column6: Táiwān hé Rìběn zhǐyǒu yī ge xiǎoshí de shíchā.
column7: Taiwan and Japan are only one hour apart.

column3: Hot spring, from 溫 "warm" + 泉 "spring". Going to one is 泡溫泉 "soak in a hot spring".
column6: Dōngtiān qù pào wēnquán hěn shūfu.
column7: Soaking in a hot spring in winter is very comfortable.

column3: Motorcycle, a loanword: 摩托 imitates the sound of "motor" and 車 is "vehicle". In Taiwan a scooter is 機車, an ordinary motorcycle 摩托車, and a big, powerful one 重機 (重型機車). You ride it with 騎: 騎摩托車.
column7: He rides a motorcycle to work.

column3: In Taiwan the everyday word for a scooter: 騎機車. An ordinary motorcycle is 摩托車. On the mainland the same characters mean a railway locomotive. In Taiwan slang, 機車 also describes a person who is fussy or annoying: 你很機車. 機 is "machine".
column6: Zài Táiwān hěn duō rén qí jīchē.
column7: Many people in Taiwan ride scooters.

column3: MRT, the metro of Taipei, Kaohsiung and other Taiwan cities: 捷 "quick" + 運 "transport". You take it with 坐 or 搭: 搭捷運, and the station is 捷運站. The mainland says 地铁 for a subway.
column7: I take the MRT to work every day.

column3: In Taiwan the usual verb for taking a vehicle: 搭捷運, 搭公車, 搭飛機; the mainland more often says 坐, which Taiwan uses too. It also means "put up, build" (搭帳篷 "pitch a tent"), and "match" in 搭配 and 搭配衣服. With a person it can mean "go along with": 搭便車 "catch a ride".
column7: I take the bus to work.

column3: Africa: 非 + 洲 "continent". 洲 has the water mark 氵 because it was first a piece of land in a river. Continents end in 洲: 亞洲, 歐洲, 美洲. 非 here only stands for a sound of the old full name 阿非利加, and elsewhere means "not" (非常 "very").
column6: Tā míngnián yào qù Fēizhōu lǚxíng.
column7: He is going to travel to Africa next year.

column3: The Americas as a continent: 北美洲 and 南美洲 are the two parts. 美國 is the United States and 美洲 is not. 美 is a sound character here, taken from "America" (亞美利加).
column7: There are many countries in the Americas.

column3: Europe: 歐 imitates the first syllable of "Europe" and 洲 means "continent". People are 歐洲人 and the EU is 歐盟.
column6: Shǔjià wǒ xiǎng qù Ōuzhōu wán.
column7: I want to go to Europe in the summer vacation.

column3: Asia: 亞 imitates the first syllable of "Asia" and 洲 means "continent". People are 亞洲人. Its regions include 東亞 "East Asia" and 東南亞 "Southeast Asia".
column7: Taiwan is in Asia.

column3: Key, counted with 把: 一把鑰匙. The second syllable is neutral, and the 匙 is read shi here, but chí in 湯匙 "spoon". 鑰 has 金 "metal" on its left. Say 忘了帶鑰匙 "forgot to bring the key".
column7: I forgot to bring my key.

column3: Neck, only in 脖子 and similar compounds. In everyday talk people say 脖子, and 頸 is the more written word (頸部 "neck area"). The ⺼ on the left is "flesh", the usual sign of a body part.
column7: His neck is very long.

column3: Neck, the part of the body between the head and the shoulders. 子 is neutral. 脖子痛 "have a sore neck". A scarf, 圍巾, goes around it.
column7: My neck hurts a lot.

column3: Ambulance: 救 "rescue" + 護 "protect" + 車 "vehicle". To call one: 叫救護車, and the number is 119 in Taiwan (also for fire) and 120 on the mainland; the police are 110 in both.
column7: Quick, call an ambulance!

column3: To cough: 他一直咳嗽 "he keeps coughing". Both characters have 口 "mouth" on their left, since it is a sound made with the mouth. The second is neutral. 感冒 "a cold" often goes with it: 感冒咳嗽.
column7: I keep coughing.

column3: To have a headache: 我頭痛. It can also mean "troublesome": 這件事很讓人頭痛 "this matter is a headache". The mainland often says 頭疼 where Taiwan says 頭痛. 痛 has 疒 "illness" for meaning.
column7: I have a headache and want to go home and rest.

column3: To register at a hospital or clinic, getting a number to see the doctor: 先掛號再看醫生. You can often 掛號 online too. It is also the word for sending a registered letter: 掛號信. 掛 means "hang" and 號 is "number".
column6: Wǒ yào xiān guàhào zài kàn yīshēng.
column7: I have to register first before seeing the doctor.

column3: Pharmacy, where you buy medicine: 藥 + 房 "shop-room". In Taiwan 藥局 is just as common, and 藥妝店 is a drugstore that also sells makeup; the mainland usually says 藥店. 房 is a "room" and also the ending for rooms and small shops.
column7: The pharmacy is next to the hospital.

column3: Save a life, and the cry for help: 救命！ A verb with its object, so it splits: 救了我一命 "saved my life". It is for real danger. Ask someone for help in daily life with 幫幫我 or 請問.
column7: Help! Someone is hurt!

column3: Rich, well-off: 他很有錢. 有錢人 means "rich person". Literally "to have money", so it works like a verb and can be negated with 沒: 沒錢 "have no money". 有錢 is a plain statement and can also be envious or ironic.
column7: His family is very rich.

column3: The boss's wife, or the woman who runs the shop herself. Common with small shops, markets and restaurants: 老闆娘 is also how customers call such a woman. The simplified 老板 writes 闆 with 板 "board". 娘 has 女 "woman" at the left.
column7: The shop owner is very nice.

column3: Shop assistant, store clerk: 店 "shop" + 員 "staff member". 員 is a common ending for people in a job: 公務員 "civil servant", 服務員, 職員. Customers call a clerk 小姐 or 先生, or just ask 請問.
column6: Zhè jiā diàn de diànyuán hěn qīnqiè.
column7: The clerks in this shop are very friendly.

column3: To reserve a seat or table: 我想訂位 "I'd like to make a reservation", The verb and object split: 訂兩個位子. It is the usual phrase for restaurants, and for trains it is 訂票. 訂 "book" + 位 "seat".
column6: Wǒ xiǎng dìngwèi, liǎng ge rén.
column7: I would like to make a reservation for two.

column3: Department store, literally "hundred goods company". Often just 百貨, the place for brand goods and a food floor, 美食街. 貨 means "goods" and has 貝 "shell, money" as its meaning part.
column7: What time does the department store open?

column3: Night market, a street market that opens in the evening, with food stalls and cheap goods, famous in Taiwan. You go to one with 逛夜市, and eat 小吃 "snacks" there. 夜 "night" + 市 "market".
column4: 我们晚上去夜市吃小吃。
column5: 我們晚上去夜市吃小吃。
column6: Wǒmen wǎnshang qù yèshì chī xiǎochī.
column7: We are going to the night market this evening to eat snacks.

column3: To stroll around the shops, to go window-shopping: 去逛街 "go shopping around", 逛了一下午的街. It is a verb with its object and can be split. The point is walking around and looking, not buying. 逛 has 辶 "walk" on the left, and 狂 for the sound.
column6: Zhōumò wǒ cháng hé péngyou guàngjiē.
column7: On weekends I often go shopping with friends.

column3: Full, no room, of a restaurant, hotel or a train: a sign 客滿 on the door means no seats are free. 今天客滿了 "we are full today". 客 "guest" + 滿 "full". 滿 has 氵 "water" on the left, as if filled to the brim.
column7: The restaurant is full today.

column3: To pay by card, literally "swipe a card": 可以刷卡嗎？ "Can I pay by card?" 刷 is "brush" or "swipe", and 卡 is a loanword for "card", as in 信用卡 "credit card". Small stalls and night markets often take cash only, so it is worth asking.
column7: Can I pay by card here?

column3: Raincoat, 雨 "rain" + 衣 "clothes". You put one on with 穿: 穿雨衣, and count it with 件: 一件雨衣. Other things for the rain: 雨傘 "umbrella", 雨鞋 "rain boots".
column7: It is raining; please wear a raincoat.

column3: Underwear, literally "inside clothes": 內 "inside" + 衣 "clothes". It covers bras, undershirts and similar; 內褲 is "underpants". The opposite is 外衣 "outer clothing".
column4: 我在百货公司买了内衣。
column5: 我在百貨公司買了內衣。
column6: Wǒ zài bǎihuògōngsī mǎi le nèiyī.
column7: I bought underwear at the department store.

column3: A tip, extra money for service: 小 "small" + 費 "fee". Tipping is not the custom in Taiwan, and many restaurants add a service charge of 10% (服務費) instead. So 不用給小費 "no need to tip". 給小費 is the verb phrase.
column6: Zài Táiwān bù yòng gěi xiǎofèi.
column7: You don't need to tip in Taiwan.

column3: Small change, coins, the money you carry loose: 找零錢 "give change", 沒有零錢 "have no small change". 零 means "zero, odd bits" and 錢 "money". A 零錢包 is a coin purse.
column7: I have no small change on me.

column3: Pocket money, allowance, the money for small expenses, usually given by parents to a child: 給零用錢. 零用 means "for odd small use". Adults also use it for money kept aside for little spending.
column4: 爸爸每个星期给我零用钱。
column5: 爸爸每個星期給我零用錢。
column6: Bàba měi ge xīngqī gěi wǒ língyòngqián.
column7: Dad gives me pocket money every week.

column3: Salad, a loanword from the English sound. 水果沙拉 is a fruit salad and 沙拉醬 is the dressing. Order with 一份沙拉 or 一盤沙拉. The characters are only for the sound.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng diǎn yī fèn shālā.
column7: I would like to order a salad.

column3: Steak: 牛 "cow" + 排 "a row, rib". A steak house is 牛排館. The waiter asks how you like it with 幾分熟: 三分熟 "rare", 五分熟 "medium", 全熟 "well done". 牛 is a picture of a bull's head with two horns.
column6: Nǐ de niúpái yào jǐ fēn shú?
column7: How would you like your steak done?

column3: Hot dog, a calque of the English: 熱 "hot" + 狗 "dog". Counted with 根 or 個: 一根熱狗. Convenience stores and night markets sell them. 熱 has 灬 "fire" at the bottom.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng chī yī gēn règǒu.
column7: I want to eat a hot dog.

column3: Steamed bun, plain and without filling, from wheat flour. Eaten for breakfast, often with soy milk (豆漿), or with a dish. A bun with meat or vegetable filling is a 包子. The second syllable 頭 is neutral. 饅 has 飠 "food" on the left and 曼 for the sound.
column6: Tā zǎocān chī mántou hé dòujiāng.
column7: He has a steamed bun and soy milk for breakfast.

column3: Mandarin orange, tangerine, used in 橘子 and for the color 橘色 "orange". It only appears in compounds. 木 "tree" is the meaning part and 矞 gives the sound.
column7: This tangerine is very sweet.

column3: Tangerine, mandarin orange, the small loose-skinned fruit: 剝橘子 "peel a tangerine". The larger orange is called 柳丁 in Taiwan, while the mainland says 橙子. Counted by weight with 斤 or with 個. 子 is neutral.
column6: Wǒ mǎi le yī jīn júzi.
column7: I bought a catty of tangerines.

column3: Mango, with 果 "fruit" for the sense and 芒 for the sound. 芒果冰, shaved ice with mango, is a well-known summer treat in Taiwan. 芒果乾 is dried mango.
column7: Taiwan's mangoes are delicious.

column3: Oolong tea, literally "black dragon tea": 烏 "black" + 龍 "dragon" + 茶. 凍頂烏龍, from Taiwan, is a well-known kind. Order a cup with 一杯烏龍茶. 烏 is a picture of a crow, which is black.
column7: I like to drink oolong tea.

column3: Soy milk: 豆 "bean" + 漿 "thick liquid". A traditional breakfast is 豆漿 with 燒餅 or 油條. It can be ordered 甜 "sweet", 無糖 "unsweetened" or 鹹 "salty". Counted with 杯 or 碗: 一碗豆漿.
column6: Wǒ zǎoshang hē yī bēi dòujiāng.
column7: I drink a cup of soy milk in the morning.

column3: Ice cubes: 冰 "ice" + 塊 "lump". Say 加冰塊 "add ice". Ordering a drink you can say 去冰 "no ice" or 少冰 "less ice". 塊 is also the measure word for pieces: 兩塊冰塊.
column7: Please don't put any ice in.

column3: Dessert, a sweet snack: 甜 "sweet" + 點 from 點心 "light snack". It is the word on café menus for cakes, puddings and the like, eaten after a meal or with tea: 點甜點 "order a dessert". 點心 is the broader word and can be savory.
column4: 吃完饭以后，我想吃甜点。
column5: 吃完飯以後，我想吃甜點。
column6: Chīwán fàn yǐhòu, wǒ xiǎng chī tiándiǎn.
column7: After the meal I'd like to have dessert.

column3: Taste, smell, flavor. It is used in 味道 "flavor" and 口味 "taste", 香味 "fragrance", 臭味 "bad smell". This is a noun and a suffix; it also appears in 意味 "meaning". 口 "mouth" is the meaning part, and 未 gives the sound (wèi).
column6: Zhège cài de wèidào hěn tèbié.
column7: This dish has a special flavor.

column3: A can, jar, tin, and the measure word for them: 一罐可樂 "a can of cola", 兩罐牛奶. 罐頭 is "canned food". 缶 on the left is an old pottery jar, and 雚 gives the sound, which matches (guàn).
column6: Wǒ mǎi le liǎng guàn kělè.
column7: I bought two cans of cola.

column3: To stir-fry, the standard cooking method for most home dishes: 炒飯 "fried rice", 炒麵 "fried noodles", 炒青菜. 炒 can also mean "to speculate" (炒股票 "play the stock market"), and "to fire someone" in 炒魷魚. 火 "fire" is the meaning part, and 少 gives the sound.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng chǎo yī ge qīngcài.
column7: I want to stir-fry a vegetable dish.

column3: To deep-fry: 炸雞 "fried chicken", 炸魚, 炸薯條 "French fries". This is the cooking sense. The same character means "to explode" with a different reading, zhà, and the word list gives zhà as Taiwan's reading for this one too. Fire 火 with a sudden 乍: the oil bursts.
column7: Mom is frying fish in the kitchen.

column3: Two uses. Placed after a list: "and so on, etc.": 蘋果、香蕉等等. And as a request: 等等！ "wait a moment!", the same as 等一下. The second use is spoken. 等 has 竹 on top for the bamboo slips of old books.
column4: 桌子上有苹果、香蕉、橘子等等。
column5: 桌子上有蘋果、香蕉、橘子等等。
column6: Zhuōzi shang yǒu píngguǒ, xiāngjiāo, júzi děngděng.
column7: On the table there are apples, bananas, tangerines and so on.

column3: Two meanings. "Not bad, so-so": 你好嗎？ 還好 "How are you? Not bad." And "luckily, fortunately": 還好你來了 "luckily you came". 還 here is read hái, not huán. It is more neutral than 很好 and does not show much feeling.
column7: Luckily you came.

column3: Just right, just in time, happen to be: 剛好 is used for timing and amount: 剛好十點 "exactly ten o'clock", 剛好夠 "just enough". 剛 is "just now", and 好 "good". The right side 刂 is a knife; the left 岡 gives the sound, which matches (gāng).
column4: 我到的时候，车刚好来了。
column5: 我到的時候，車剛好來了。
column6: Wǒ dào de shíhou, chē gānghǎo lái le.
column7: When I got there, the bus had just arrived.

column3: Wow!, a cry of surprise or admiration: 哇，好漂亮！ It can also sound like a baby's cry or vomiting, as the word list notes. It is spoken, not written formally, and has 口 "mouth" on the left, like most such sounds.
column7: Wow, it's so big!

column3: To need, require, mostly in 需要 "need" and 需求 "demand": 你需要幫忙嗎？ "Do you need help?" Also in 不需要 "no need". It stays in compounds and on notices. The 雨 "rain" on top fits the idea of need: plants need rain.
column7: Do you need help?

column3: Must, have to, used almost only in compounds: 必須 "must", 無須 "no need". 你必須早點睡 "you must sleep earlier". 必須 is firmer than 要 or 得. The same character was first the word for "beard" (彡 "hair" beside 頁 "head"), which is written 鬍鬚 today.
column7: You must go to bed earlier.

column3: To soak, steep, and "bubble". 泡茶 "make tea", 泡麵 "instant noodles", 泡澡 and 泡溫泉 "soak in a bath, in a hot spring", 泡沫 "foam". The verb is for anything left in hot water or other liquid. 氵 gives the sense of liquid, and 包 the sound (bāo and pào).
column6: Wǒ xiǎng pào yī bēi chá.
column7: I'd like to make a cup of tea.

column3: And, moreover, but almost always inside 而且 "furthermore": 這家店便宜，而且好吃. Alone, it is written style: 暫且 "for the time being", 並且 "and also". 且 is an old picture, perhaps of a stone altar or a sacrificial vessel, and is also the right-hand part of 祖.
column4: 这里的菜好吃，而且很便宜。
column5: 這裡的菜好吃，而且很便宜。
column6: Zhèlǐ de cài hǎochī, érqiě hěn piányi.
column7: The food here is tasty, and it is cheap too.

column3: For example, let's say, spoken, used to introduce an example: 比方說，你想去哪裡？ Like 例如 and 舉例來說, but more casual. 比方 means "comparison, analogy" and 說 "say". The 方 is neutral.
column7: For example, you can eat fruit.

column3: Other, another, placed directly before a number or measure word: 另一個 "another one", 另兩個 "another two", 另有 "there is also". 另外 is the form used for "besides" in a sentence. It points to a different thing, not "more of the same".
column6: Lìng yī ge rén yě lái le.
column7: Another person came too.

column3: Kind, appearance, way, in compounds: 一樣 "the same", 這樣 "like this", 怎麼樣 "how is it", 樣子 "appearance". It is also a measure word for kinds of things: 兩樣菜 "two dishes". 木 "tree" is the meaning part and 羕 the sound.
column7: What do you think?
